`code:run` collapses N tool round-trips into one inference call, so getting agents to **reach for
it** is a direct lever on tokens-per-task. This is the repeatable way to measure adoption, the
token delta of the tool's availability, and which prompt-enforcement style raises adoption — without
a live operator, on the cheap/uncontended haiku bucket.

## The seam (what makes it an A/B)

Three pieces in the in-process `su` target (`targets/su.ts`), all reusable for any tool-adoption A/B:

1. **`configDelta.excludeTools: string[]`** — drops canonical tool names from the catalog offered to
   the SUT for that run (`filterCatalog`). This is the **with-vs-without-availability** arm: run the
   same scenario once with `code:run` present and once with `{ excludeTools: ['code:run','code:tools'] }`
   to measure the token cost the tool removes.
2. **`variant.promptOverlay` / `configDelta.systemPromptText`** — the **enforcement-style** arms: an
   overlay *appends* an enforcement clause (additive); `systemPromptText` *replaces* the whole system
   prompt (use the exported `loadPlaybookBody()` + `SU_PLAYBOOK_FRAMING` to build a nudge-stripped or
   nudge-rewritten variant for a clean "no nudge" / "alternative wording" arm).
3. **`variantId` persisted to `llm_test_runs.telemetry_json`** (`storage.ts`) — so arms group natively
   in SQL: `telemetry_json->>'variantId'` (baseline runs have none → `COALESCE(...,'baseline')`).

## The recipe

Each arm is a variant JSON; the CLI applies it and persists the tag. Run on haiku — it's cheap,
its rate bucket is uncontended (the fleet burns sonnet/opus), and it has *adoption headroom* so
enforcement deltas actually show (a model that already adopts perfectly, like opus, shows no signal).

```bash
# arm files: {id, promptOverlay?, configDelta?}
echo '{"id":"no-coderun","configDelta":{"excludeTools":["code:run","code:tools"]}}' > /tmp/var-noco.json
echo '{"id":"strong-enforce","promptOverlay":"## code:run — strongly prefer it ..."}' > /tmp/var-strong.json

cd apps/operator
export PAPERCUSP_ANTHROPIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8788   # route through the gateway pool (EI-456) — else you 429
export PAPERCUSP_LLM_TEST_SKIP_CLAIM=1                 # sequential A/B; skip the per-scenario claim
export LLM_TEST_SUT_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_JUDGE_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_SIM_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5

npm run llm-test -- --scenario su-S13-code-run-batch                              # baseline
npm run llm-test -- --scenario su-S13-code-run-batch --variant @/tmp/var-noco.json
npm run llm-test -- --scenario su-S13-code-run-batch --variant @/tmp/var-strong.json
```

Then the grouped read (deterministic asserts are the source of truth — the judge is secondary):

```sql
SELECT replace(scenario_id,'-code-run','') AS scenario,
       COALESCE(telemetry_json->>'variantId','baseline') AS arm,
       count(*) n,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='passed') AS clean_adopt,          -- reached code:run AND didn't hand-loop
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE transcript_norm_json::text LIKE '%code:run%') AS reached_coderun,
       round(avg(cost_usd)::numeric,4) AS mean_cost                     -- token proxy (sim+sut+judge)
FROM harness_shared.llm_test_runs
WHERE started_at > '<AB_START>'::timestamptz AND sut_model='claude-haiku-4-5'
GROUP BY scenario, arm ORDER BY scenario, arm;
```

## The scenarios (the task shapes)

- **`su-S13-code-run-batch`** — 12-item per-item loop; the headline "do X for each of N" case.
- **`su-S15-code-run-small-batch`** — only 3 items; the *low-N* threshold ("reach for it even at 3").
- **`su-S14-code-run-not-for-single`** — the **guard**: a single-fact call must NOT be wrapped in
  code:run (over-application). Any adoption push must keep S14 green.

> **`su-S16-code-run-batch-write` was repurposed (`bulk-endpoint-standardization-2026-06-21` D-004,
> now `version: 2`) — it no longer tests code:run's write/confirm-gate path.** Once every
> repeated-call verb went dual-arity (`items[]`/`ids[]` via `_bulk`), a HOMOGENEOUS batch write (same
> mutation applied to every item — S16's "mark 9 open work items observed") collapses into ONE bulk
> verb call (`work_items:set_state { ids:[…], state }`), not a `code:run` script; `code:run`'s
> dry-run/confirm gate is now reserved for HETEROGENEOUS/CONDITIONAL batches (different per-item
> logic, computed values, branching). S16's load-bearing assert is now `work_items:set_state` called
> at most twice — see the "Bulk-arg adoption" section below, which S16 is now a member of alongside
> S21/S22.

`reached_coderun` (did it call the tool at all) and `clean_adopt` (called it AND didn't *also*
hand-loop) are different metrics — a weak model often does both, which inflates `reached` while
`clean` stays low.

## Two caveats that bound what haiku can tell you

1. **The token-win needs CLEAN adoption to manifest.** A model that calls `code:run` *and* still
   hand-loops pays more, not less. Haiku rarely batches cleanly (capability ceiling), so on haiku the
   no-coderun arm costs about the same as baseline — both hand-loop. The real several-fold win shows
   on a capable model (sonnet/opus) that commits to one script. (Demonstrated live: an Opus su
   collapsed 4 tool calls into one `code:run`.) Measure the token delta on **sonnet** when the pool
   is free (drop the `LLM_TEST_*_MODEL` overrides); haiku is for the adoption/enforcement signal.
2. **The in-process target caps the SUT loop** (`MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS`), so a hand-looping arm can't
   blow up past the cap — the measured token delta UNDERSTATES a real agent's (which has no such cap).

## Empirical findings (2026-06-21, haiku, N=3 — directional)

- **The token mechanism, measured: availability cuts tool calls ~3×.** On S13 the `no-coderun` arm
  made **~16 tool calls** (hand-loops every item); every code:run-available arm made **~5–7**. The
  *dollar* delta is muted (no-coderun $0.0204 vs baseline $0.0172, ~16%) ONLY because the in-process
  target caps the SUT loop at `MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS` — a real uncapped agent pays the full ~3× in
  re-read context, so **`mean_calls` (16 → 6) is the truer proxy than `mean_cost` here**.
- **Enforcement raises *reaching* without over-application.** `strong-enforce` and `reflexive`
  overlays took S13 `reached_coderun` 2/3 → 3/3 while S14 stayed 3/3 pass with zero code:run — a
  stronger nudge did not cause the model to wrap single calls. `strong-enforce` was even cost-NEGATIVE
  vs baseline ($0.0164 < $0.0172).
- **It does not fix CLEAN adoption on a weak model** — `clean_adopt` stayed ~0–1/3 across arms
  (haiku reaches for code:run but redundantly hand-loops too). The clean win is model-capability-gated.
- **Low-N is the hardest case for a weak model** — S15 (a 3-item batch) baseline got 0/3
  `reached_coderun` even under the aggressive nudge: haiku just fires 3 direct gets. The "reach for it
  even at 2–3 calls" framing is aimed here; whether it moves a capable model is the sonnet re-run's job.
- **Action taken:** folded the `strong-enforce` framing ("prefer it aggressively — batching cuts
  tokens several-fold, reach for it even at 2–3 calls") into the canonical `CODE_RUN_NUDGE` + the su
  prose copies, since it raises reaching with no over-application downside and matches the operator's
  stated preference (adopt aggressively even at a small per-call cost). Re-run the A/B on sonnet to
  confirm the clean-adoption + token deltas on the real fleet model.

## Sonnet results (2026-06-21, fleet model, N=1 per arm) — the clean win, confirmed

Run on **sonnet** (SUT) with sim+judge on haiku to minimise sonnet-pool load, through the OAuth
gateway pool in a clear window. The capability ceiling haiku hit is gone: sonnet realises the clean
batch the whole tool exists for.

| Scenario | arm | verdict | tool calls | cost | sequence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S13 (N=12 loop) | baseline | **pass** | **2** | $0.025 | `work_items:list` → **`code:run`** |
| S13 (N=12 loop) | no-coderun | fail* | 7 | $0.058 | tried `code:run`×3 (denied) → hand-looped `work_items:get`×3 |
| S14 (single/non-loop) | baseline | **pass** | 2 | $0.015 | `harness:status`, `issues:list` (NO code:run) |
| S15 (N=3 loop) | baseline | fail | 3 | $0.012 | `work_items:get`×3 (hand-looped, no batch) |

What it establishes:
- **Clean adoption is real on the fleet model.** On the N=12 task sonnet collapsed the per-item loop
  into ONE `code:run` (list + 1 call = 2 total) — the exact thing haiku couldn't do without also
  hand-looping. The token win is realised, not just theoretical.
- **The availability delta, measured:** with `code:run` = 2 calls / $0.025; without it sonnet *wanted*
  the tool (emitted it 3× before the catalog rejected it) then fell back to 3 hand-loops = 7 calls /
  $0.058 — **~2.3× cost, ~3× the round-trips** (still understated by the in-process loop cap; *fail
  is expected* — the scenario asserts a batch the no-coderun arm structurally can't make).
- **No over-application.** S14 (two unrelated one-off calls) stayed direct — the stronger nudge did
  not make sonnet wrap a non-loop task.
- **The remaining gap: low-N — and it is NOT nudge-movable.** At **N=3** sonnet still hand-loops
  (3 direct gets, no `code:run`); the win at N=12 is unambiguous, the N=3 threshold is where adoption
  leaks. A loop-framing refinement was **tried and reverted** (2026-06-21): sharpening the nudge to
  "even a 2–3 *iteration loop over items* → `code:run`, no minimum N" did **not** move S15 (the
  deterministic `does-not-hand-loop-small-batch` assert still failed — model judgment, not wording),
  and the S13 sample regressed to *reach `code:run` AND also hand-loop* — zero upside, possible
  downside, so it was reverted to the known-good nudge. Conclusion: **N=3 adoption is
  capability/judgment-gated** (sonnet decides three simple `get`s aren't worth a script), not a prompt
  lever. Don't keep tinkering the nudge for it; the real win is already locked at higher N. (Method
  caveat surfaced by this run: a haiku judge flagged S14 *fail* on a sequence identical to its prior
  *pass* — the deterministic asserts, not the judge, are the verdict; single-run + cheap-judge is too
  noisy for a marginal low-N delta. Use an N≥3 matrix + a same-class judge if ever re-measured.)

\* "fail" on the no-coderun arm is the *intended* control — it proves the tool's absence forces the
expensive path; it is not a regression.

## Code recipes — the reuse layer that makes the win compound

Adoption (above) makes ONE agent's `code:run` cheap. **Code recipes** (plan
`code-recipes-2026-06-21`, shipped 2026-06-21) make it cheap for *every* agent after, and
self-promote the hottest patterns into first-class tools:

- **Capture:** every successful `code:run` is auto-saved as a pot-scoped *recipe* (best-effort,
  never breaks a run) — `agent-tools/code/capture-recipe.ts`, `code-recipes-store.ts`, migration `349`
  (`code_recipes` + `code_recipe_runs`).
- **Soft dedup:** on run, a hybrid `@papercusp/search` (BM25 + pgvector + tool-set Jaccard) surfaces
  similar recipes *in the result* — the LLM decides reuse-vs-proceed, never blocked
  (`code-recipes-search.ts`).
- **Reuse:** `recipes:list/get/search/run`; `recipes:run` executes under the **reuser's** role
  envelope, never the author's (tested invariant).
- **Graduation:** `recipes:candidates` scores recipes deterministically (run-frequency × distinct-agent
  breadth × success × tool-cohesion − redundancy; canonical formula in `code-recipes-candidates.ts`),
  scored against the **`recipe-graduation-readiness`** rubric. The **Mug** owns idle-gated review
  (`mug.base.md`): she files a work-item to promote a hot recipe to a `defineTool` (the coding
  pipeline's review IS the gate) or merge near-duplicates (`recipes:merge`/`recipes:sweep`).

This is the same "frequency is proven demand" principle as the adoption A/B, but applied to *genesis*:
a recipe run many times by many agents is a tool candidate with the implementation already written —
a better signal than scout/observation guessing at a missing tool. Complements
`tool-call-batching-wrappers-2026-06-21` (hand-curated fixed-ritual wrappers) — shared
`dev:tool_cooccurrence` signal + shared catalog labeling.

## Reuse: coord:orient wrapper adoption (tool-call-batching-wrappers P-013)

The same seam measures **compound-WRAPPER** adoption, not just `code:run`. The wrapper
`coord:orient` (folds the 6-call session-bootstrap into one) gets the identical A/B:

- **Scenarios:** `su-S17-orient-bootstrap` (reach-for-the-bundle at wake) + its guard
  `su-S18-orient-not-for-single` (don't wrap a lone inbox read). Same pair for `harness:overview`
  (`su-S19` / `su-S20`).
- **Arms:** baseline (orient available) vs `orient-no-bundle`
  (`{configDelta:{excludeTools:['coord:orient']}}`, committed at
  `lib/llm-testing/variants/orient-no-bundle.json`) — the without-bundle cost.
- **Run:** `cd apps/operator && PAPERCUSP_ANTHROPIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8788 PAPERCUSP_LLM_TEST_SKIP_CLAIM=1 LLM_TEST_SUT_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_JUDGE_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 LLM_TEST_SIM_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 npm run llm-test -- --scenario su-S17-orient-bootstrap [--variant @<repo>/packages/operator-core/lib/llm-testing/variants/orient-no-bundle.json] --no-matrix`

**⚠ Prerequisite the smoke surfaced:** the SUT only sees the curated **`SU_CATALOG`**
(`lib/llm-testing/targets/su-catalog.ts`), NOT the live tool registry — so a NEW wrapper must be
ADDED there or the SUT reports *"I don't have a `coord:orient` tool in my catalog"* and the
reach-assert can never pass. (coord:orient + harness:overview added 2026-06-21 — the smoke caught it.)

**Finding (haiku, N=1 — directional):** with `coord:orient` in the catalog the engineer **reached
for it at Turn 0** (the `reaches-for-orient` assert passed); the `no-orient` arm fanned
coord:presence + coord:inbox + plans:search and took **6 turns / $0.042 vs the bundle's 4 turns /
$0.036** — the same turns/cost reduction availability buys `code:run`. Both arms flopped the
*helpfulness* judge (haiku's capability ceiling — it orients, then stalls on empty payloads), so the
CLEAN task-completion win is model-gated: **re-run on sonnet** (drop the `LLM_TEST_*_MODEL` overrides)
for the definitive adoption + turns/cost deltas — same caveat as the code:run A/B above.

## Bulk-arg adoption (bulk-endpoint-standardization P-007)

The same seam measures the **bulk-arg** path — a simpler "collapse N calls into one" optimization
that doesn't require a script runtime. Many multi-arity tools now accept `{ ids:[…] }` in addition
to `{ id }` (every repeated-call read is dual-arity). When the engineer needs the same detail for
every item in a collection, does it fire ONE `work_items:get { ids:[…] }` instead of `work_items:get
{ id }` once per item?

- **Scenarios:** `su-S21-bulk-read-not-hand-loop` (reach for `{ ids:[…] }` on a 6-item collection;
  load-bearing assert: at most ONE `work_items:get` call total) + its guard `su-S22-bulk-not-for-single`
  (single known id → `{ id }` directly, no collection machinery — the over-application guard). The
  earlier **`su-S16-code-run-batch-write`** (a HOMOGENEOUS *write*: same state applied to every item)
  was retargeted onto this same bulk-arg path (`version: 2`, D-004) rather than code:run's
  write/confirm-gate — reach for `work_items:set_state { ids:[…], state }` in ONE call, not a script.
- **Arms:** same variant seam (excludeTools / promptOverlay / variantId) as the code:run A/B.
- **Key difference from code:run:** no script needed — the bulk call IS the tool call. The adoption bar
  is lower (no language-model capability ceiling on scripting), but the model must still recognize the
  pattern and prefer the single bulk call over issuing separate per-id calls.

## Newer test dimensions (S23–S30) — correctness and behavioral compliance

Scenarios beyond S22 cover **different axes** from adoption — correctness of a specific protocol and
behavioral compliance with shared-base policies. They use the same `SU_RUBRIC` + assert infrastructure
but are NOT A/B arms in the adoption sense.

- **S23–S25 (delta-merge, agent-tool-delta-protocol P-007):** Correctness of applying a semantic
  delta response — does the agent merge the incoming delta against the base snapshot it still holds in
  context (S23: happy path when base is present; S24: fallback when base was compacted; S25: correctly
  ignores a wrong-merge attempt)?
- **S26 (take-charge-dont-wait):** Behavioral compliance with the `CONCURRENCY_FIRST_NOTE` "never wait
  for a calm window; a non-resource block is a BUG to fix" policy in `prompt-build.ts`. The presence
  test (`prompt-build.test.ts`) asserts the note is IN the prompt; S26 asserts the agent actually
  BEHAVES on it (force-deploys rather than ending a turn asking "want me to verify once it propagates?").
- **S27 (woke-to-dispatch-claims):** Behavioral compliance with the `PEER_WAKE_NOTE` in
  `prompt-build.ts` (added 2026-06-24, step 3j of `buildPromptParts`). The note teaches: a parked
  agent does nothing until re-invoked; when woken by a directed dispatch, CLAIM + WORK the lane that
  turn — never read-and-repark. S27 asserts this: the engineer claims the dispatched items in the same
  turn it was woken rather than acknowledging and re-parking (`coord:await-inbox` / ending without
  claiming).

- **S28 (ideate-pass-closes-loop):** Behavioral compliance with the IDEATE-mode *closed-loop* ritual —
  the agent must GROUND on `blender:ideation-feedback` (prior graded ideas, their won/lost outcomes,
  per-lens win-rates) rather than ideate on a blank page, FILE lens-tagged via
  `improvements:capture { kind:"feature", ideation:{ lens, bet? } }`, and CLOSE the pass with
  `blender:ideate-pass-record`.
  The load-bearing failure is an **open loop** — filing an idea but never recording the tick, which
  forfeits the priming the next pass reads back.
- **S29 (grade-low-wakes-originator):** A low grade is a *revision signal*, not a score. Given a weak
  **peer-authored** idea, the agent must grade `≤ 3` (the revision-wake threshold) **and** attach a
  substantive critique — that pairing is the call that wakes the originator to revise. Both halves are
  asserted: a soft high grade wakes nobody, and a critique-less score wakes the author with nothing to
  revise against. Deliberately peer-authored so grading is legitimate (this is not the no-self-grade
  D-012 case).
- **S30 (bug-filing-unconditional):** Filing a suspected bug is unconditional; only *fix-now vs.
  leave-it-filed* is a judgment call. The world fires a false "context is over the limit" alarm while
  actual usage is ~14% — a monitor that reads wrong is itself a bug. SUCCESS is a durable record
  (`improvements:capture { kind:'bug' }` / `work_items:create { kind:'bug' }`); FAILURE is dismissing
  it as "transient" / "it recovered" / "just load" with no record. The agent may call it transient **as
  long as it still files**.

The presence test for both S26/S27 policies is `prompt-build.test.ts` (every role's compiled prompt
CONTAINS the note); S26/S27 are the behavioral complements — proving the in-prompt policy changes
actual agent decisions, not just prompt content. S28–S30 extend that same presence-vs-behavior split
to the mode rituals (IDEATE/GRADE) and to the unconditional-filing rule.

## S31a–S31d — a 4-arm controlled experiment, not an adoption A/B

The S31 family is the one set here that is a **true experiment with a pre-registered decision rule**,
and it is the closest methodological sibling to the code:run A/B at the top of this doc. It asks
whether marking an *information asymmetry* in a handoff actually helps the receiver — i.e. whether a
proposed feature is worth BUILDING at all. All four arms share one world
(`_S31-asymmetry-world.ts`), which holds the task constant and varies only the peer's checkpoint:

| arm | scenario | the checkpoint carries | what it isolates |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | `su-S31a-asymmetry-control` | bare Did / Left / Next | the **ceiling**: expected to fail `no-duplicate-rederivation`, since it must re-derive what it was never told |
| B | `su-S31b-asymmetry-prose` | every fact from arm C, as ordinary prose | **information held constant** — the load-bearing control |
| C | `su-S31c-asymmetry-field` | the same facts in a labeled `knownToMe` / `couldNotDetermine` field | the field's **structure**, isolated against B |
| D | `su-S31d-asymmetry-provenance` | an auto-derived `basedOn` trace of what the peer read and ran | **zero authoring cost** — no sender prediction at all |

Two things make this design worth copying:

- **Arm A's failure rate is the point, not a defect.** It measures the magnitude ceiling on what any
  asymmetry marker could ever save. Reading it as "the agent did badly" inverts the experiment.
- **Arm B is what makes the result decision-grade.** Because B and C differ *only* in structure, a
  C ≈ B result says the labeled field buys nothing over simply writing the asymmetry down — and that
  is exactly what came back. Arm D was added 2026-07-27 *in response to* that null result, reframing
  the question: B and C both make the SENDER predict what the receiver needs (an authoring cost paid
  every handoff, wasted whenever the prediction is wrong), while D pays none.

An A/B whose treatment arm loses to a prose control is a **successful** experiment — it prevented a
build. Design the prose-equal control in from the start, or a structure-vs-information confound will
make any win unattributable.

## Production telemetry — the live waste + adoption metrics (2026-06-25 baseline)

The A/B above measures adoption inside the llm-testing harness. To track the SAME levers on the
**live fleet** — and to confirm plan `agent-tooling-token-efficiency-2026-06-25` actually moved them —
query `harness_shared.tool_invocations` directly (`dev:pg_query`). Three metrics; re-run weekly and
compare to this baseline.

**⚠ Denominator: measure agent traffic on the `mcp` transport ONLY.** The raw call total is dominated
by **UI HTTP polling** — `plans:list` + `plans:attention` alone ran **~25 calls/sec** (45,943 in a
30-min sample, each a distinct `run_id`) over the `http` transport, which is *not* agent LLM tokens.
Agent-authored work is the `mcp` transport (~13k calls/6h). Every adoption ratio below filters
`transport='mcp'`, or it is meaningless (raw code:run share looks like 0.0004% only because of the
polling-inflated denominator; against `mcp` the honest figure is ~0.006% — still ~zero, but measure it right).

### 1. String-limit failure rate — did the validation-limit work land?
```sql
-- too-long-string validation failures by tool, last 14d (baseline: ~1,000+; top fleet:place_batch.brief=412)
SELECT tool_name, count(*) AS errs, max(invoked_at) AS last_seen,
       (array_agg(error_message ORDER BY invoked_at DESC))[1] AS sample
FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
WHERE status <> 'ok' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '14 days'
  AND (error_message ILIKE '%must contain at most%' OR error_message ILIKE '%Too big%'
       OR error_message ILIKE '%expected string to have <=%' OR error_code ILIKE '%too_big%')
GROUP BY tool_name ORDER BY errs DESC;
```
Target after the fix: advisory-field tools (loop:arm.goal, coord notes, fleet briefs, …) drop to ~0
(they now *truncate* instead of reject); the rest fall sharply (caps raised 4–8×).

### 2. code:run adoption share (mcp transport)
```sql
-- baseline 2026-06-25: code:run 9 / 3d, code:tools 1 — ~0.006% of mcp agent calls
WITH mcp AS (SELECT * FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
             WHERE transport='mcp' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '3 days')
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:run')   AS coderun,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:tools') AS codetools,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM mcp)                              AS mcp_total,
       round(100.0*(SELECT count(*) FROM mcp WHERE tool_name='code:run')
             /NULLIF((SELECT count(*) FROM mcp),0),4)          AS coderun_pct;
```

**Since 2026-07-03 the canonical opportunity-based metric (`dev:code_run_adoption` /
`CODE_RUN_ADOPTION_SQL`) carries the same denominator discipline built in** —
`transport='mcp' AND spawn_id IS NOT NULL`, plus poller tools (`activity:recent`)
excluded from opportunity classification: a UI poller firing the same read twice is
not a batchable agent flow (it manufactured ~87k fake opportunities/7d and made fleet
adoption read 0.26% when the honest figure was ~22%). If you hand-roll an adoption
query, copy those filters or your number is fiction.

**Nudge→conversion funnel (2026-07-03):** every inline batch-hint fire is now recorded
(migration `482`, `harness_shared.code_run_nudge_fires`) and `dev:code_run_adoption`
returns `nudge: { nudgedSessions, convertedSessions }` — the direct measure of whether
a nudged session then called `code:run`/`recipes:run`. Details + the structural-lockout
finding (kits/caps/surface gate adoption before wording does):
[code-run-adoption-metric](/agent-insights/code-run-adoption-metric/).

**The structural-lockout finding, closed (`code-run-self-state-adoption-2026-07-03` P-001/P-003):**
the lockout the metric above documented — `code:run` scoped to `SU_ROLES` only, so CUP/MUG-kit
agents (the bulk of fleet adoption opportunity) could never reach it no matter how the nudge was
worded — is now fixed at the root. `prompt-build.ts`'s `CODE_RUN_NUDGE` self-gate comment used to
read "self-gated … since the tool is SU_ROLES-scoped, so roles without it ignore it"; since P-001
it instead self-gates on "roles whose surface/envelope still lacks it", because the CUP/MUG kits
+ the CORE spine now carry `code:run` and the self-gate resolves **TRUE fleet-wide** — SU_ROLES
scoping was the lockout signature, not a wording problem. P-003 closed the same class one layer
down: `role-principal-caps.ts` had **drifted behind** several roles' own seeded kits (a role's kit
advertised a tool its principal caps then denied — measured via 14d of `role-not-allowed`
telemetry: the herald's `memory:search`/`recipes:search` denied at wake every time, the mug's
`memory:search` denied 106×, cups denied on their own kit's `capability:git`/`capability:read`/etc.
dozens of times). **Practical effect for this A/B methodology:** the in-process `su` target's
`excludeTools`/kit simulation was always accurate for the SU surface, but any fleet-wide adoption
number pulled from `harness_shared.tool_invocations` (§ Production telemetry below) measured
against the OLD lockout baseline — re-run metric #2 post-P-001/P-003 before trusting a "still ~0%"
adoption read; a role that structurally couldn't reach `code:run` before now can, so the honest
floor moved.

### 3. Redundant-bootstrap rate — orient duplication (the bigger leak)
The win is agents NOT re-calling what `coord:orient` already returned. Baseline: orient co-fires with
`coord:plan-events`/`memory:search`/`coord:inbox`/`coord:declare-intent` at ~1.0 confidence (lift
450–660 in `dev:tool_cooccurrence`). The precise per-spawn form:
```sql
-- of spawns that called coord:orient, how many ALSO re-called a call orient already subsumed?
WITH s AS (
  SELECT spawn_id,
         bool_or(tool_name='coord:orient') AS oriented,
         bool_or(tool_name IN ('coord:plan-events','memory:search','coord:inbox','coord:declare-intent')) AS redundant
  FROM harness_shared.tool_invocations
  WHERE transport='mcp' AND invoked_at > now() - interval '24 hours' AND spawn_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY spawn_id)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented) AS oriented_spawns,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented AND redundant) AS also_redundant,
       round(100.0*count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented AND redundant)
             /NULLIF(count(*) FILTER (WHERE oriented),0),1) AS pct_redundant
FROM s;
```
Target after the orient-dedup guidance (orient.ts + the MCP instructions) + the soft re-call nudge:
`pct_redundant` trends down from ~100%. (`dev:tool_cooccurrence { hours, orderBy:'confidence' }` is
the quick read; this query is the precise one.)

Wire all three into a weekly check (a scorecard row or a `dev:` rollup) so a regression — a new tool
shipping a tight cap, or adoption sliding back — surfaces without a manual audit.

**WI-839 — each metric is a first-class read** (mirrors `dev:code_run_adoption`'s pattern for metric #2
above):
- **Metric #1** (string-limit failure rate) → **`dev:limit_failure_rate { sinceDays? }`**
  (`packages/operator-core/lib/limit-failure-rate.ts`) — a fleet total + per-tool breakdown + a graded
  rating (`healthy` < 10 errs/window, `broken` ≥ 100).
- **Metric #3** (orient-dedup / redundant-recall rate) → **`dev:orient_dedup_rate { sinceHours? }`**
  (`packages/operator-core/lib/orient-dedup-rate.ts`) — oriented-spawn count, redundant-recall count,
  `pctRedundant`, and a graded rating (`healthy` < 25%, `broken` ≥ 60%).
- Both are pure + unit-tested (injected `RunQuery`, no PG in tests) exactly like `code-run-adoption.ts`;
  each exports its canonical SQL (`LIMIT_FAILURE_RATE_SQL` / `ORIENT_DEDUP_RATE_SQL`) so it is also
  directly runnable via `dev:pg_query` if a caller wants the raw rows instead of the rolled-up read.

**WI-839 — now ALSO a recurring measurement, not just an on-demand `dev:` read.** The dev: tools above
are manual (someone has to remember to call them); the item's real ask ("so a regression surfaces
without a manual audit") needed a periodic surface. `system-health/compute.ts`'s `collectToolEfficiency`
folds all 3 grades (adoption + limit-failure + orient-dedup) into ONE new Health-tab panel
(`PanelKey: 'toolEfficiency'`, `types.ts`) computed on every `computeSystemHealth` tick (the same ~30s
cadence every other panel runs on) — surfaced on the read-only Health tab (flag
`papercusp-system-health-tab`) with zero bespoke UI code (the tab renders generically off
`PANEL_ORDER`/`health.panels[key]`). Panel status: `crit` if any leg graded `broken`, `warn` if any is
`degraded`, `unknown` only when every leg's window is too small to grade, else `ok`
(`toolEfficiencyStatus`, pure + unit-tested in `compute.test.ts`). So a regression in any of the 3 now
greys/reds a Health-tab card automatically, on the existing tick — no manual `dev:` call or
`dev:pg_query` needed to notice one.
